title: Flow reservoir: adaptive degradation and tenant admission for Dedicated routing
creator: Marco Ruiz
description:
Problem: Dedicated pools sometimes experience transient overloads when tenant mix shifts (bursting tenants + long-running heavy-context requests). The current admission shapers and shedder heuristics are either too blunt (drop whole tenants) or too conservative (no shedding until queues blow past SLOs). This leads to customer-visible p99 spikes and missed throughput guarantees for committed tenants.

Proposal summary: Implement a tenant-aware "flow reservoir" admission layer upstream of dedicated pools that maintains small per-tenant elastic buffers (reservoirs) and a shared overflow pool. The reservoir grants admission tokens proportional to a tenant's committed throughput + earned credits. When bursts occur, the system degrades gracefully by: 1) draining shared overflow before evicting tenant tokens, 2) applying service-class soft-shedding rules (reduce max inflight, reject early with structured error), and 3) routing overflow to cheaper, compatible model variants or fallback regions when configured. The design couples admission decisions with autoscaler signals so that transient load triggers quick soft-degrades while longer sustained increases prompt autoscale.

Key behaviors: generate per-tenant token buckets with elastic headroom, implement shared overflow reservoir with weighted fairness, integrate with Dedicated routing policies for immediate fallback routing, and expose metrics/trace hooks for tracing admission decisions to Console.

Why different: Instead of a single global queue or strict per-tenant hard caps, Flow Reservoir blends reserved guarantees with elastic shared capacity and explicit early-reject semantics to keep latency SLOs for high-priority tenants while maximizing overall throughput and enabling smarter autoscaling triggers.
acceptance_criteria: Committed tenants maintain >= 95% of their guaranteed throughput under 2x burst up to configured pool limit (verified in staged load test)
P99 latency for P0 routes does not regress more than 10% compared to baseline during a synthetic mixed-burst scenario
Admission decisions are annotated in traces and visible in Console route-level dashboard with per-tenant counters
Autoscaler receives and acts on the new burst indicator metric within 30s and scales up when sustained demand exceeds autoscale thresholds
test_plan: Create staged dedicated pool with mixed tenant classes and synthetic traffic profiles (steady + bursty)
Run chaos scenarios: node OOM, delayed KV cache, regional egress failure and validate graceful degradation paths
End-to-end benchmark: measure throughput guarantees, queue depths, drop rates, and fallback routing throughput (Grafana dashboard)
Run canary on a single small cluster for 48h with real traffic shadowing and strict monitoring alerts
rollout_plan: Feature flag gated: flow_reservoir_v1 toggled per-cluster
Stage 1: enable for internal QA tenants in staging and run benchmarks (2 weeks)
Stage 2: enable for low-traffic production pool with monitoring and automatic rollback on SLO breach (48h canary)
Stage 3: phased rollout to all Dedicated pools with tenant opt-in for fallback routing (2-4 weeks)
Post-rollout: 30-day observation window and retrospective; promote to default after acceptance
implementation_notes: Admission path must be non-blocking and O(1) per request; use atomic counters and sharded reservoirs to avoid global locks
Integrate with existing admission middleware (ratequeue) but separate token accounting to allow simultaneous evaluation of soft-shed and hard-shed policies
Expose structured rejection payload (x-reject-code: RESOURCE_OVERFLOW, diagnostics token) for SDKs to display fallback options
Keep reservoir sizes configurable per-tenant via Console and support dynamic overrides tied to contracts
Ensure persistence of earned credits across short reconnect windows but avoid long-term credit hoarding (decay window configurable)
